text: The cold arrived like an enemy offensive of its own. A Siberian front swept down over the high plateau. In a single day the temperature dropped by more than forty degrees. At night it fell to twenty below zero. Then thirty below. On the worst nights it approached forty below. The wind howling through the passes made it feel even colder. Nothing worked the way it should. Gun oil turned thick as glue. Carbines jammed after a single shot. Browning Automatic Rifles fired slowly or not at all. Mortar baseplates cracked when they struck the frozen earth. Artillery shells fell short because the powder burned slowly in the cold. Batteries died. Truck engines had to be run all night or they would never start again. Blood plasma froze solid in its bottles. Medics carried morphine syrettes in their mouths to keep them from freezing. Canned rations froze into blocks of ice. A Marine who warmed a can over a small fire would eat hot food around a frozen core. Dysentery spread through the ranks. Frostbite was everywhere. Feet sweated inside rubber boots called shoe-pacs during the day and froze at night. Fingers lost all feeling inside thick mittens. Men who pulled off a glove to fire a rifle could lose the skin of their hand to the frozen steel. The ground was frozen nearly a foot deep. Shovels bounced off it. Men used explosives just to blast out a foxhole. Others built walls of rock and packed snow and lay behind them all night. The terrain made everything worse. The reservoir sat on a high plateau ringed by peaks. Ridges climbed steeply from the road on both sides. Whoever held the high ground could fire straight down onto anything that moved along the MSR. And the road itself was barely wide enough for a single truck. In places it clung to cliffs with a sheer drop on one side. Yet the cold did not choose sides. The Chinese suffered even more. Many wore quilted cotton uniforms and canvas shoes. Some had no gloves at all. They had marched for weeks on handfuls of rice and frozen potatoes. Whole units lost more men to frostbite than to American bullets. Later some Chinese soldiers would be found frozen to death in their fighting positions with their weapons still in their hands. This was the stage for one of the most brutal battles of the twentieth century. Two armies would fight on a frozen plateau where the weather killed without mercy. And on the night of November twenty-seventh the bugles began to sound.
